transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Um, yeah… I’m probably making it sound bigger than it is, but what really made me come in is I’ve been getting jumpy at work. Like if a door slams or someone rolls a suitcase fast across the lobby, I kind of jump like it’s happening again, and it takes me a minute to get my heart to settle down. I just figured maybe I should ask someone about it, if that makes sense.
When you say 'it’s happening again,' can you tell me what you mean by that? Are you thinking of a specific event or experience that comes back to you when you get startled?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but there was this guest at the counter who kind of leaned over and knocked some of the equipment toward me. And sometimes, out of nowhere, I’ll just get this picture of that moment in my head—like him coming over the counter, stuff coming at me—even if I’m just answering a normal phone call. It’s not all the time, but… that’s what I mean, I guess.
Do you find that these memories of the incident come up even when you're not thinking about it, or do they usually happen in response to something specific like a sound or situation?

It’s… a little of both, I think. Sometimes there’s a sound or something at the desk that sets it off, but other times it just sort of pops in when I’m not trying to think about it—like I’ll be answering a totally normal phone call and suddenly I get that picture of him leaning over the counter and the equipment coming toward me. It’s not constant or anything, but yeah, it does happen out of nowhere sometimes.
Since that incident happened, have you found yourself avoiding certain people, places, or situations that remind you of it?

A little, yeah. I mean, I’m still going to work and everything, so I don’t want to make it sound like I’m avoiding my job… but I’ve been taking the back hallway when I can. Walking past that spot in the lobby where it happened makes my chest tighten, and I just kind of want to get away from it. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Since that incident happened, have you noticed any lasting feelings — like fear, anger, or maybe even guilt — that seem to stick around even when you're not thinking about the event?

I don’t know… not in a big way, I don’t think. I mean, I get a little shaken when I’m reminded of it, but I wouldn’t say I’m walking around angry or scared all day.

Maybe I’m a little embarrassed that it got to me as much as it did, but… I don’t know if that counts. I’m trying not to make too much of it.
Since the incident, have you had any ongoing feelings of fear, guilt, or anger — even if they’re not constant — that seem to linger after you’ve had one of these reminders?

I’m not sure I’d call it ongoing, exactly. After something reminds me, I can feel kind of unsettled for a bit, maybe embarrassed that I reacted, but it usually fades. I don’t think I’m carrying around fear or anger or guilt in any big way… at least I haven’t really noticed that. Does that make sense?
Since the incident, have you noticed any changes in your mood or the way you see yourself — like feeling overly negative, detached from others, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t think so… not really. I mean, I’ve maybe been a little more quiet than usual, but I wouldn’t say I feel detached or like I’ve lost interest in things.

I still want to do my normal stuff. I might just be a little distracted sometimes. But mood-wise, I think I’m mostly okay. Is that helpful?

Since the incident, have you had any thoughts about yourself or the world that have stayed with you—like thinking you're unsafe, the world feels dangerous, or you could have done something differently?

I don’t think so… not in any way that’s really stuck with me. I mean, right after it happened I probably had the normal “what if” thoughts, like anyone would, but I’m not walking around thinking the world is dangerous or that I’m not safe.

And I don’t think I’m blaming myself, either. At least not that I’ve noticed. I’m trying to be fair about it, but… no, I wouldn’t say those thoughts have really stayed with me. Is that answering what you mean?
Since the incident, have you had any ongoing emotional reactions—like fear, anger, or guilt—that seem to stick around even when you’re not actively thinking about the event?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I can get a little shaken when something brings it back up, but when I’m not thinking about it, I’m not sitting there feeling scared or angry or guilty all the time.

At least, I don’t think I am. I’ve been trying to pay attention, and it seems like those feelings don’t really stick around. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Since the incident, have you found it hard to experience positive emotions, or noticed that you're more negative about yourself or the world than before?

I don’t think I’ve had a hard time feeling positive, no. I mean, I’m maybe a little more distracted or not totally myself every second, but I can still laugh at things and enjoy stuff.

And I wouldn’t say I’m more negative about myself or the world. I’m trying not to make too much of it, but… no, that doesn’t really feel like what’s happening for me. Does that make sense?
Since the incident, have you had any ongoing trouble sleeping, concentrating, or felt unusually irritable, even when you're not thinking about the event?

I wouldn’t say I’m irritable, really, and sleep is… not the main thing, I guess. But concentrating has been a little harder than I’d like to admit.

At the desk, I used to move through reservations pretty smoothly, and lately I’ll catch myself rereading the same screen or second-guessing simple stuff, like which room note to enter first. It’s not like I can’t do my job, but it’s slower and I feel kind of embarrassed by it. Is that the sort of thing you’re asking about?
Outside of reminders related to the incident, do you often feel on edge or unusually alert, like you're always watching for something to happen?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, if something directly reminds me of it, I might tense up for a minute, but just in general, walking around or at work, I’m not constantly scanning for danger or anything like that.

At least I haven’t noticed myself doing that. If anything, I’m trying to keep things normal. Does that answer it?
Since the incident, have you noticed that you’re more easily upset or that your emotions feel more intense than they used to, even about everyday things?

Maybe a little, yeah. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m yelling at people or anything, because I’m really not trying to be difficult.

But I’m usually pretty careful with coworkers, and lately I’ll hear myself giving these short answers over really small stuff… like if someone asks me to repeat a confirmation number, I’ll snap it back more sharply than I mean to. Then I feel bad right away.

So, I guess my emotions might be a bit closer to the surface than usual. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Since the incident, have you noticed that you're more easily upset or that your emotions feel more intense than they used to, even about everyday things?

A little, yes… though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. I’m not, like, blowing up at people.

It’s more that I’m usually pretty careful with coworkers, and lately I’ll catch myself giving these short answers over tiny things. Like if someone asks me to repeat a confirmation number, I’ll snap it back sharper than I meant to. Then I feel bad right after.

So, yeah, I guess I’m more easily upset than usual, just in small ways.
Since the incident, have you noticed any persistent feelings of numbness, detachment, or a reduced interest in activities you used to care about?

I don’t think so, no. I mean… I’ve had moments where I feel kind of tired of talking about it, or I’d rather just keep busy, but I wouldn’t say I feel numb or detached from people.

I’m still doing the normal things I usually care about, at least as much as I can. So I don’t think that’s really been happening. Is that okay to say?

Since the incident, have you found yourself thinking in ways that feel overly negative—like believing you’re in danger more than you actually are, or that you could have done something differently to prevent it?

I don’t think so… not really. I mean, I’ve had normal “what if” thoughts here and there, but I’m not walking around thinking I’m constantly in danger or anything like that.

And I don’t think I’m blaming myself for it. At least, not in any big way. I’ve mostly been trying to just be sensible and get back to normal. Does that answer it?
Since the incident, have you had any persistent emotional reactions — like ongoing fear, anger, or guilt — even when you're not reminded of it?

Not really, no. I mean, I get a little tense if something brings it up, but just sitting around out of nowhere feeling afraid or angry or guilty… I haven’t really noticed that.

I’m maybe a bit more on edge than I’d like, but I wouldn’t call it ongoing fear or guilt. I think that’s accurate.
Since the incident, have you had any days where you just feel unusually down, upset, or emotionally reactive, even if nothing specific happens to remind you of it?

I wouldn’t say so, no. I mean, I have normal ups and downs, and maybe I’ve been a little more tired or quieter some days, but not like… suddenly really down or reacting strongly for no reason.

If something reminds me of it, that’s different, I guess, but just out of nowhere? I haven’t really noticed that. I hope that makes sense.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation of jumpiness and startle response to specific stimuli leads to consideration of trauma- and stressor-related disorders, anxiety disorders, and other stress-related conditions.

F34.8 was ruled out as the patient denies significant mood changes or depressive symptoms. The other conditions remain possible given the reported intrusive memories, avoidance behaviors, and startle response.

The patient reports heightened emotional reactivity and irritability in response to reminders of the event, but no persistent negative emotional state or cognitive changes outside of trauma-related triggers. This maintains the differential between PTSD (F43.10), panic disorder (F40.00), and generalized anxiety disorder (F40.210). No disorder is ruled out at this time.

The patient reports increased emotional reactivity and irritability in response to minor stressors, which supports the presence of an anxiety or stress-related disorder. However, symptoms do not clearly localize to only one specific disorder. The constellation of symptoms continues to support a differential including PTSD (F43.10), generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), and possibly adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.21). No specific phobia (F40.00) was endorsed strongly in this turn, but it remains as a less likely candidate.
